This value, which represents the maximum basal metabolic rate recorded for the species, is consistent with the moderate energetic demands expected of a small, seed-eating heteromyid rodent inhabiting the arid Great Basin. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive, resting individuals during their inactive phase, ensuring that the oxygen consumption reflected true basal metabolism rather than the costs of thermoregulation or digestion. For a rodent of its body size, this metabolic rate is relatively low, a pattern commonly observed in desert-adapted mammals that rely on energy conservation as a strategy for surviving in resource-poor environments. These physiological data provide a critical baseline for understanding how Microdipodops pallidus manages its energy budget across seasonal extremes.

Females produce between 2 and 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 7 pups per litter], with the frequency of litters estimated at approximately 1 per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 per year]. The reported maximum reproductive rate was observed under controlled thermal conditions of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], which approximates the warm spring temperatures that trigger the onset of breeding activity in natural populations. Litter size appears to be influenced by maternal body condition and local resource availability, with females in better condition producing larger litters near the upper end of the documented range. The combination of moderate litter size and low annual frequency allows this species to rapidly increase population numbers when conditions are favorable.

Subsequent growth is rapid, with females eventually attaining an ultimate adult body mass of 16.8 grams [Wwi = 16.8 grams], though individuals may range from 10.3 to 16.8 grams depending on seasonal food availability and reproductive status. The disparity between the tiny neonate and the adult female underscores the intense period of somatic investment that occurs during the suckling stage, during which pups must gain over fifteen times their birth weight to approach independence. This growth trajectory is energetically demanding for the lactating female, who must balance the costs of milk production against her own maintenance requirements in an environment where food resources are often unpredictable.

The developmental timeline of the Pale kangaroo mouse proceeds through several clearly defined stages under the species' preferred thermal regime. At an ambient temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], which approximates the species' thermoneutral zone, puberty is attained at 50 days after birth [tp = 50 days after birth]. The weaning period, estimated at 29 days from birth [tx = 29 days from birth], marks the transition from complete nutritional dependence on maternal milk to the onset of independent foraging at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. The relatively short weaning period combined with early puberty enables a high intrinsic rate of population increase, which is critical for a species occupying ephemerally productive desert habitats.

Longevity and the pace of life-history events in the Pale kangaroo mouse reflect its adaptation to an unpredictable arid environment. The maximum recorded lifespan is 5.5 years [am = 5.5 years] under conditions maintained at approximately 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], indicating that individuals can persist across multiple breeding seasons despite the physiological challenges of desert life. The combination of a short gestation period, early weaning, and rapid pubertal maturation, paired with a moderately long adult lifespan, describes a life-history strategy oriented toward opportunistic reproduction during brief windows of resource abundance. This suite of traits positions the species as a classic example of a desert-adapted rodent capable of rapidly exploiting temporary pulses of productivity.
